name: Tea tree oil
short: Reviews say tea tree oil is toxic if swallowed (central nervous system depression, pneumonitis) and can irritate skin and cause allergy; trial side effects were minor except topically at 25% or more.
text: A toxicity review says that anecdotal evidence from almost 80 years of use suggests topical use is relatively safe, with minor, self-limiting and occasional adverse events, but that published data indicate tea tree oil is toxic if swallowed in higher doses and can irritate the skin at higher concentrations; allergic reactions occur in predisposed people and may be due to oxidation products formed when the oil is exposed to light or air. The same review says that data from individual components suggest the oil could be developmentally toxic if swallowed at higher doses. A review of 159 reports of adverse reactions possibly caused by the oil in a World Health Organization database, 16 of them serious, concluded that it should never be taken by mouth because it can lead to central nervous system depression and pneumonitis, that skin disorders may occur with topical use, and that contact allergies are difficult to predict. A contact allergy review found positive patch test reactions in 0.1% to 3.5% of people routinely tested and nearly 100 allergic patients in case reports and case series, mostly after applying pure oil. In a systematic review of 46 randomised trial articles, side effects were reported in 60% of studies and were minor, except where the oil was applied topically in concentrations of 25% or more. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
